query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A predictive framework that explicitly incorporates the effects of defect scattering and oxygen‐induced modifications on the local electronic structure into ab initio conductivity calculations will yield more accurate temperature‐dependent electrical conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr (including samples with ~1 wt.% oxygen) than conventional models based on perfect, defect‐free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy synthesized with its intrinsic microstructural defects and containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen impurity.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply a modeling approach that combines quantum‐mechanical electronic structure calculations (e.g., using disorder averaging methods such as CPA) with corrections for defect and oxygen impurity scattering—potentially calibrated by machine learning—to account for local relaxations.
generation.conditions: The model’s predictions are evaluated in two separate temperature regimes: a low-temperature regime (approximately 0–200 K) where defect and impurity scattering predominantly affects carrier mobility, and a high-temperature regime (approximately 300–1200 K) where phonon scattering couples with oxygen-induced effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Inherent alloy disorder including microstructural defects and interstitial oxygen atoms that perturb the local atomic and electronic structure.
generation.mechanism: By explicitly incorporating defect- and oxygen-induced scattering processes, the model modifies the computed electronic band structure and carrier scattering rates, thereby yielding predictions that more closely mirror the real conduction behavior over the measured temperature ranges.
generation.predicted_outcome: The enhanced model is expected to reduce the average prediction error of electrical conductivity (relative to standard perfect-crystal analytical methods) to within approximately ±10–15% of experimental values in both temperature regimes, compared to errors exceeding 20% from conventional models.
generation.baseline: Existing analytical models that assume perfect, defect‐free crystals and neglect the scattering effects introduced by microstructural defects and oxygen impurities.
generation.boundary: Applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloys with oxygen contamination levels around 1 wt.% and within the temperature ranges of 0–200 K and 300–1200 K. Predictions outside these impurity levels or temperature ranges remain untested.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of error reduction and the robustness of the model in different defect density regimes remain uncertain and will depend on the quality of defect characterization and calibration data.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with a controlled ~1 wt.% oxygen contamination. Measure the electrical conductivity using high-precision four-probe techniques at selected temperatures in the low (e.g., 50 K and 150 K) and high (e.g., 600 K and 1100 K) regimes. Compare these measurements with predictions made by both the defect-inclusive model and conventional perfect-crystal models.
measurements: Quantification of defect density and oxygen distribution (using TEM, atom probe tomography, or similar techniques)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the defect-inclusive predictive framework does not improve the conductivity prediction error to within ±10–15% (i.e., if its predictions are not significantly better than those from conventional models with errors >20%) in either the low- or high-temperature regime, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The crucial point of our approach is to enhance the simulation efficiency by employing the most suitable method for different sets of properties. Specifically, CPA’s quantum mechanical treatment of solid solutions and its analytical nature eliminates finite-size cell effects and sampling errors related to random atomic configurations, making it excel in calculations of the concentration dependence of properties that are relatively insensitive to local relaxations, such as elastic constants and misfit volumes. In comparison to supercell calculations with MLIPs, CPA is especially superior in accuracy when dealing with abrupt changes of the Fermi-surface topology, which is often encountered in bcc alloys and can have a significant impact on the concentration dependence of properties. On the other hand, ab initio based MTP methodology surpasses CPA in dealing with defects and special geometries, such as surfaces, due to its capability to incorporate local atomic relaxations.

cited_evidence.kind: web:2.4. Approaches to Alloy Design and Selection
cited_evidence.text: Each approach to alloy design (selection) that has been discussed above would give an alloy composition for which solidification path, volume fractions of phases and phase equilibria at different temperatures could be calculated, provided thermodynamic data was available. This task is not possible currently, for the reasons discussed in the introduction. Using knowledge gained from on-going research it is possible to make some informed predictions for the selected alloys. The latter and the calculated (predicted) properties can be tested experimentally. For example, the alloy A should have βNb5Si3 as its primary phase, in its microstructure tetragonal Nb5Si3 and Nbss should be stable at 1500 °C but not the C14 NbCr2 Laves and A15 intermetallic phases and the alloy should not pest. The alloy B should have βNb5Si3 as its primary phase, eutectic with Nbss and Nb5Si3 should form (see below), in its microstructure tetragonal Nb5Si3, Nbss (most likely solid solution with no Si) and A15 intermetallic should be stable at 1500 °C but not C14 NbCr2 Laves phase and the alloy should not pest.

In RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs, the CC bcc solid solutions with Ge+Sn and Al, Cr, Hf, Mo, Ti and W additions are (i) stable (Figure 1) and (ii) Si free [,]. It is suggested (a) that single phase bcc solid solution RCCAs or RHEAs with above elements would be stable at high temperatures. Furthermore, given that Ge+Sn with Al, Cr, Hf, Mo and Ti improve oxidation at pest and high temperatures [,,,] it is suggested (b) that these RCCAs or RHEAs would also be oxidation resistant. For B containing RM(Nb)ICs, RM(Nb)ICs/RCCAs, RM(NB)ICs/RHEAs, RCCAs and RHEAs it is suggested to study the contamination with oxygen of their solid solutions and to find out if there is a relationship between the parameter δ and the oxygen concentration, see Boron Containing RM(Nb)ICs in Section 3.2.1.

drafts.hypothesis: An advanced predictive method that integrates defect‐tolerant modeling—including explicit treatment of oxygen impurities and non‐perfect lattice structures—will yield more accurate estimates of conductivity in bulk HfNbTaTiZr than traditional analytical models that assume perfect crystals.
drafts.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr, with two specimen conditions: one nearly ideal (defect‐free assumption used in analytics) and one containing ~1 wt.% oxygen impurities.
drafts.intervention: Apply a machine learning–augmented simulation framework that is trained on datasets generated from simulations (e.g., first‐principles or molecular dynamics) including common defects and oxygen impurities, rather than only considering perfect crystal structures.
drafts.conditions: Measurements and predictions are focused on two temperature regimes: a low-temperature regime (nearly 0–200 K) and a high-temperature regime (300–1200 K).
drafts.structural_mediator: The presence of oxygen (and associated defect structures) alters local bonding environments, which increases phonon/electron scattering mechanisms not captured in perfect crystal models.
drafts.mechanism: The new predictive approach improves accuracy by incorporating defect-induced scattering and lattice disorder effects into its training data. This allows it to account for the temperature‐dependent influence of oxygen impurities on conductivity, yielding predictions that are more consistent with experimental observations in both the low- and high-temperature regimes.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The defect‐inclusive approach is expected to reduce the prediction error relative to conventional analytical methods (which assume defect‐free crystals), achieving notably closer agreement with experimental conductivity measurements (e.g., error reduction on the order of 15% or more) in both temperature regimes.
drafts.baseline: Traditional analytical predictions that assume perfect, defect‐free crystals and neglect the scattering effects of even low levels of oxygen impurity.
drafts.boundary: The method is expected to be applicable for bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloys with up to about 1 wt.% oxygen impurity, within the temperature limits of near 0–200 K and 300–1200 K. Its reliability outside these bounds (e.g., for higher impurity levels or temperatures beyond 1200 K) remains to be tested.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two series of bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set synthesized as near-ideal crystals and another with 1 wt.% oxygen intentionally introduced. Apply the new predictive approach to generate conductivity predictions over the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes. Then, measure the actual conductivity (or comparable transport property) across these temperature ranges using appropriate cryogenic and high-temperature setups.
measurements: Conductivity (or electrical/thermal transport property) as a function of temperature for near-ideal and oxygen-doped specimens.
Microstructural characterization to confirm oxygen content and defect distributions (e.g., using TEM or XRD).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the defect‐inclusive predictive approach does not reduce the discrepancy between predicted and measured conductivity by at least approximately 15% relative to conventional analytical predictions (across both temperature regimes), or if its predictions consistently fail to capture the effect of the 1 wt.% oxygen impurity, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A data-driven, machine‐learning predictive model that explicitly incorporates the effects of microstructural defects and a 1 wt.% oxygen impurity will improve the thermal conductivity predictions for bulk HfNbTaTiZr over conventional analytical models that assume a perfect crystal lattice, especially in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K temperature regimes.
drafts.material_initial_state: Bulk high-entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr prepared in near-equiatomic proportions; one set of samples is essentially defect‐controlled (defect‐minimized) while another set is doped with 1 wt.% oxygen.
drafts.intervention: Develop and apply a machine-learning model trained on both experimental measurements and simulation data that include defect- and oxygen-induced scattering effects, rather than relying on perfect-crystal analytical formulations.
drafts.conditions: Measurements are taken in the low-temperature regime (0–200 K) and high-temperature regime (300–1200 K). The oxygen-doped sample enables evaluation of the model’s ability to account for impurity-based structural disorder.
drafts.structural_mediator: Microstructural defects, including oxygen-induced impurity sites, that affect phonon and possibly electronic scattering in the material.
drafts.mechanism: By incorporating experimentally observed defect densities and oxygen impurity effects into its input features, the machine learning model is expected to capture non-linear scattering processes that alter thermal conductivity. This approach overcomes the limitation of traditional analytical methods which assume ideal, defect-free crystals.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The ML model will yield predictions of thermal conductivity that more closely match experimental measurements in both temperature regimes, with improvement over traditional perfect-crystal based analytical predictions. In particular, better agreement is anticipated for the oxygen-doped samples where impurity-related scattering is significant.
drafts.baseline: Traditional analytical models assuming perfect, defect-free crystal structures, which have been shown to deviate from measured conductivities particularly when oxygen impurities and defect-induced scattering are present.
drafts.boundary: This hypothesis is limited to bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with low to moderate defect levels and impurity concentrations (up to about 1 wt.% oxygen). Its applicability outside the specified temperature ranges (0–200 K and 300–1200 K) or to other alloy systems remains untested.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens: one with near-perfect crystallinity and one doped with 1 wt.% oxygen. Measure the thermal conductivity across the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes. Apply the newly developed ML predictive model as well as conventional analytical models to predict the thermal conductivity over these ranges.
measurements: Thermal conductivity as a function of temperature
Structural characterization (e.g., defect density, impurity distribution) via microscopy or diffraction
Chemical composition verification (ensuring ~1 wt.% oxygen in doped samples)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML model does not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement (e.g., a reduction in prediction error of at least ~20%) over traditional analytical predictions for either temperature regime or if its predictions fail to capture the marked differences observed in the oxygen-doped samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A predictive framework that explicitly incorporates defect scattering and oxygen-induced local electronic structure modifications into ab initio conductivity calculations will more accurately predict the temperature-dependent electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr (including real, contaminated microstructures) compared to conventional models based on perfect, defect‐free crystals.
drafts.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy as synthesized with inherent microstructural defects and 1 wt.% oxygen contamination.
drafts.intervention: Implement a modeling approach that marries quantum-mechanical electronic structure calculations (e.g., using CPA or similar methods) with defect and impurity scattering corrections (possibly enhanced by machine learning calibration) to account for local relaxations and oxygen contamination effects.
drafts.conditions: Measurements and predictions are made in two distinct regimes: a low-temperature regime (0–200 K), where defect and impurity scattering govern carrier mobility, and a high-temperature regime (300–1200 K), where electron-phonon interactions coupled with oxygen-related defect effects dominate.
drafts.structural_mediator: The presence of defects and interstitial oxygen that perturb the local atomic and electronic structure, thereby altering carrier scattering rates and density of electronic states near the Fermi level.
drafts.mechanism: By accounting for the effects of defects and oxygen contamination on the electronic band structure and scattering mechanisms, the approach modifies predictions for carrier mobility and conductivity. In the low-temperature regime, enhanced defect scattering introduces characteristic deviations from perfect-crystal behavior, while at high temperatures, oxygen-induced variations adjust the electron-phonon interaction strength, leading to a more realistic temperature dependence.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The new predictive model is expected to reduce the average error in predicted electrical conductivity to within ±10–15% of experimental values in both temperature regimes, outperforming standard analytical predictions (which assume defect-free crystals and typically deviate by >20%).
drafts.baseline: Standard analytical models that compute conductivity based on perfect, defect‐free crystal assumptions, which do not accurately capture the impact of oxygen contamination or inherent microstructural defects.
drafts.boundary: Applicable only for bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloys with oxygen contamination up to approximately 1 wt.% and for measurements in the temperature ranges 0–200 K and 300–1200 K. Accuracy outside these conditions (or for markedly different defect densities) remains uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with controlled 1 wt.% oxygen contamination. Measure the electrical conductivity as a function of temperature over the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes using high-precision methods (e.g., a four-probe technique). Compare these measurements with predictions from (a) the new defect-inclusive model and (b) traditional perfect-crystal models.
measurements: Defect and oxygen distribution characterization (e.g., via TEM or atom probe tomography)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the defect-inclusive predictive framework does not improve the conductivity prediction error to within ±10–15% (i.e., if its predictions remain as poor as or worse than the conventional perfect-crystal models with errors >20%) in either temperature regime, then the hypothesis is falsified.

drafts.hypothesis: A predictive model that integrates quantum‐mechanical disorder averaging (using, for example, the coherent potential approximation) together with temperature‐dependent electron–phonon and defect (oxygen) scattering corrections will accurately reproduce the electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr across both the low temperature regime (0–200 K), where defect scattering dominates, and the high temperature regime (300–1200 K), where phonon scattering is dominant. This approach will overcome the inaccuracy of traditional analytical predictions that assume perfect, defect‐free crystals.
drafts.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr, including a realistic oxygen contamination level of approximately 1 wt.%.
drafts.intervention: Apply a hybrid predictive method that combines first‐principles electronic structure calculations using disorder averaging (e.g., CPA) with additional scattering models (and possibly ML‐based corrections) to incorporate both electron–phonon interactions and the scattering due to oxygen-induced defects.
drafts.conditions: Temperature regimes from 0 to 200 K and from 300 to 1200 K on bulk samples containing ~1 wt.% oxygen; the model is intended for samples where the inherent chemical disorder and trace defect concentrations are representative of real experimental conditions.
drafts.structural_mediator: The intrinsic chemical disorder of the refractory high‐entropy alloy combined with oxygen interstitials (defects) that modify local scattering rates and electronic density of states.
drafts.mechanism: By explicitly accounting for the effects of alloy disorder and oxygen contamination, the model modifies the electronic band structure and adds realistic scattering mechanisms (electron–phonon and defect scattering) that are temperature dependent. This produces conduction predictions that better match observed behaviors compared to standard analytical models that assume ideal crystals.
drafts.predicted_outcome: The model is expected to predict electrical conductivity values within an approximate error margin of less than 15% of measured values across the two temperature regimes. In the 0–200 K regime, conductivity variations will primarily reflect defect scattering effects, while in the 300–1200 K regime, phonon scattering will dominate, both captured by the model.
drafts.baseline: Existing analytical predictions based on perfect, defect‐free crystals that do not incorporate temperature‐dependent scattering from oxygen and other defects, leading to systematic deviations from experimental measurements.
drafts.boundary: The model is applicable for bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples with typical oxygen contaminations around 1 wt.%; its accuracy in specimens with significantly different impurity levels (e.g., ultra‐high purity or excessively contaminated samples) or beyond 1200 K remains unverified.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimens with controlled oxygen contamination of approximately 1 wt.%. Measure the electrical conductivity using a four‐probe method at selected temperatures in the 0–200 K regime (e.g., 50 K and 150 K) and in the 300–1200 K regime (e.g., 600 K and 1100 K). Compare the experimentally measured conductivity values with those predicted by the new hybrid model.
measurements: Electrical conductivity at 50 K, 150 K, 600 K, and 1100 K.
Characterization of oxygen content by chemical analysis to ensure ~1 wt.% contamination.
Verification of microstructural disorder via electron microscopy or diffraction.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the predicted electrical conductivity deviates by more than approximately 15% from the measured values at one or more of these key temperatures, then the hypothesis that the hybrid predictive approach improves accuracy over conventional defect‐free analytical models is falsified.
